steps.title: Store and find by key
steps.content: A hash table stores key-value pairs. A hash function maps a key to an array index, making lookup and insertion O(1) on average.
steps.example: A student ID can be the key and the student's record the value.

steps.title: Why collisions happen
options: Two keys map to the same table index
steps.explanation: Different keys can produce the same hash-table index. The table must handle the collision.

steps.title: Handle collisions
steps.content: Separate chaining stores multiple entries in a bucket, often as a list. Open addressing searches for another available slot using probing.
steps.example: If keys 12 and 22 both hash to index 2, chaining keeps both entries in bucket 2.

steps.title: Average lookup
steps.prompt: What is the average lookup time in a well-sized hash table?
steps.explanation: With a good hash function and controlled load factor, lookup is O(1) on average.

steps.title: Understand the worst case
steps.content: If many keys collide, a bucket can become long and operations may degrade to O(n). A good hash function distributes keys, and resizing helps keep the load factor controlled.
steps.tip: Hash table operations are average O(1), not guaranteed O(1) in every case.

questions.prompt: What does a hash function do?
options: Maps a key to a hash value/index
questions.explanation: A hash function maps a key to a location in the table.

options: Two keys map to the same index
questions.explanation: A collision occurs when distinct keys map to the same table index.
Separate chaining stores collided entries together in a bucket.

questions.prompt: What is average lookup time in a well-designed hash table?
questions.explanation: Expected lookup is O(1) under a suitable distribution and load factor.

questions.prompt: What can happen in the worst case with many collisions?
questions.explanation: If entries accumulate in one bucket or probe sequence, lookup can degrade to linear time.
